prompt.context: Your client is PSG, a Latin American private bank. It is one of the oldest banks within the region and, despite continuous growth throughout the years, its revenues have been constantly declining the past five years. The CEO of PSG is worried and has called you and your team to help her reverse this trend. PSG has company presence in most Latin American countries and is not interested in expanding to other regions. PSG has two types of competitors: other large traditional banks and smaller start-up banks with increasing presence in retail spaces; the latter are seen as an important threat due to important product innovation, especially in credit card products and incentives. PSG divides its operations into Retail (personal credit cards, personal loans), Commercial (small, medium, and large firm products), and Products and Markets (trading, project finance, forex, derivatives). We will not focus on deposits. PSG had yearly revenues of around $10B in 2005. The strategy team has determined that it can invest $500M per year for two years to reverse the observed continuous decline in income of 2% per year. By 'reverse', the CEO means to have at least no decline: forecasts project a similar decline the next two years. Profit margins (in %) have remained constant.
prompt.question: How would you advise PSG to reverse its declining revenues over the next two years, given a budget of $500M per year?

clarifying_info.q: Is the decline driven by revenues, margins, or both?
clarifying_info.a: Focus on revenues; profit margins have remained constant overall and by segment.
PSG operates in most Latin American countries and is not interested in expanding to other regions.

clarifying_info.q: What does 'reverse the decline' mean specifically?
clarifying_info.a: The CEO wants at least no decline — i.e., flat revenues or better — over the next two years. Current forecast projects a continued 2% annual decline.

clarifying_info.q: Is the $500M investment per year a hard cap?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, $500M per year for two years is the budget available.

exhibits.title: PSG Bank Revenues ($B)
exhibits.shows: Two charts: (1) PSG total bank revenues in $B from 1999 to 2005; (2) PSG bank revenues broken down by segment (Retail, Commercial, Others) from 2001 to 2005.
exhibits.data: Total revenues: ~$11B in 1999-2000, declining to ~$10B by 2005. Segment breakdown (2001-2005): Retail declines from ~$6B to ~$4B; Commercial and Others together grow modestly over the same period.

exhibits.title: PSG Bank Retail Revenue Breakdown ($B)
exhibits.shows: Breakdown of PSG Retail segment revenues by sub-segment (credit cards, personal loans, and other retail) from 2001 to 2005.
exhibits.data: Credit card revenues decline sharply by approximately $500M per year over the five-year period. Personal loans and other retail sub-segments are small and grow slowly.

framework: Identify whether the problem is revenue, margin, or both — confirm it is a revenue (growth) problem with stable margins
Segment the revenue decline: Retail vs. Commercial vs. Products and Markets
Diagnose the root cause within the declining segment (Retail, specifically credit cards)
Identify growth levers: Organic (quantity/price within existing segments, new products, new clients) vs. Inorganic (M&A, JVs, acquisitions)
Assess external factors: regulation, competitive dynamics (start-up banks gaining share via product innovation)
Evaluate feasibility and cost of recommended initiatives against the $500M/year budget
Formulate recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 1. What is happening to PSG's revenues, and what is the primary driver?
questions.guidance: Candidate should quickly confirm the ~2% annual decline in total revenues (shortcut: ~$11B in 2000 to ~$10B in 2005 is ~10% over 5 years, i.e., ~2%/year). The key insight is that the RETAIL segment is the main driver of decline — it fell from ~$6B to ~$4B in five years (roughly -10%/year), while Commercial and Others grew at roughly +9-10%/year. An excellent candidate notes Retail is now ~40% of revenue and that even slowing (not reversing) Retail's decline could achieve the goal, especially combined with continued growth in other segments.

math.setup: Total revenue decline: ~$11B (2000) to ~$10B (2005). Retail: ~$6B (2001) to ~$4B (2005).
steps: Total decline: ($11B - $10B) / $11B ≈ 9-10% over 5 years ≈ ~2% per year
Retail decline: ($6B - $4B) / $6B ≈ 33% over 4 years ≈ ~9.1% per year (exact)
Commercial + Others: grew ~9.3% per year (exact)
Forecast: continuing to lose ~$200M/year (2% of ~$10B) for next two years without intervention
math.answer: Primary driver of decline is the Retail segment, falling ~$500M/year; Commercial and Others are growing but not enough to offset.

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 2. What is the most urgent issue within Retail, and how does it relate to the overall objective?
questions.guidance: Candidate should rapidly identify that credit card revenues are declining by ~$500M per year. Personal loans and other retail sub-segments are small and growing slowly — even doubling them in two years would not offset credit card losses. The key so-what: if PSG simply stops the credit card decline, it would essentially meet the CEO's 'no decline' objective for the next two years. Candidate should pivot to what can be done about credit cards.

math.setup: Credit card revenue decline ~$500M/year. Overall revenue decline target to halt: ~$200M/year.
steps: If credit cards continue losing $500M/year, other segments must grow $300M/year net just to reach flat — very difficult
If credit card decline is stopped entirely, other segments' modest growth would more than offset any remaining drag
Therefore stopping the credit card decline alone is sufficient to meet the 2-year objective
math.answer: Stopping the ~$500M/year credit card revenue decline is the single most impactful lever to meet the 'no decline' objective.

questions.prompt: Brainstorm: What can PSG do to stop the decline in credit card revenues?
questions.guidance: See brainstorming section. Candidate should structure ideas into Quantity (retain/acquire customers), Price (revenue per customer), and Other/Inorganic buckets. Strong candidates mention loyalty/miles programs specifically given the competitive context provided.

questions.prompt: The client team found that PSG is losing credit card customers due to competitors offering miles-per-dollar-spent loyalty programs. Competitors offering miles programs hold 1/3 of the total credit card market; PSG also holds 1/3. The team estimates PSG could retain 100% of customers and revenue with a similar program. How would you estimate PSG's potential annual expense for a comparable miles loyalty program?
questions.guidance: Candidate should first outline the approach (bottom-up preferred since top-down lacks cost-per-flight data). Key steps: estimate total market credit card spend, isolate the 1/3 held by miles-offering banks, compute miles accumulated, apply redemption rate, split domestic/international flights, apply cost per flight negotiated with airlines, scale to PSG's equal market share. The critical so-what: compare $312M/year program cost to the $500M/year budget — it fits, and it would stop the $500M/year credit card revenue bleed.

math.setup: Bottom-up market sizing of PSG's annual cost to run a miles loyalty program matching competitors.
steps: Latin American population in PSG countries: ~80M
Population eligible for credit card (ages 18-80, ~75% of total): 80M x 75% = 60M people
Credit cards per person: assume 1
Monthly spend per person: assume $1,000/month
Total monthly credit card market spend: 60M x $1,000 = $60B/month
Market share of banks offering miles programs: 1/3 → monthly spend generating miles: $60B / 3 = $20B/month
Miles accumulated per $1 spent: 1 mile → 20B miles/month accumulated
Miles effectively redeemed: 50% utilization rate → 10B miles/month redeemed
Split: 80% domestic, 20% international
Domestic: 10B x 80% = 8B miles; avg miles per domestic flight = 50,000 → 8B / 50,000 = 160,000 flights/month; avg negotiated cost per domestic flight = $100 → 160,000 x $100 = $16M/month

International: 10B x 20% = 2B miles; avg miles per international flight = 100,000 → 2B / 100,000 = 20,000 flights/month; avg negotiated cost per international flight = $500 → 20,000 x $500 = $10M/month
Total monthly spend by miles-offering banks: $16M + $10M = $26M/month
PSG has equal market share (1/3), so PSG's expected monthly expense: $26M/month
PSG's annual expense: $26M x 12 = $312M/year
math.answer: Estimated annual cost of a comparable miles loyalty program for PSG: ~$312M/year, which is within the $500M/year budget.

brainstorming.prompt: What can PSG do to stop the huge decrease in credit card revenues?

categories.name: Quantity — Retain existing customers
ideas: Loyalty programs (e.g., miles per dollar spent)
Exclusivity partnerships with institutions (e.g., airlines, retailers)
Enhanced customer service and relationship management

categories.name: Quantity — Capture new customers
ideas: Discounts or sign-up incentives to open new accounts
Target new demographic or income segments currently underserved

categories.name: Price — Increase revenue per customer
ideas: Increase interest rates on revolving balances (check price elasticity)
Bundles or cross-subsidies to increase card usage across different store types

categories.name: Price — Decrease default rate
ideas: Sell high-default-probability accounts to other institutions

categories.name: Other / Inorganic
ideas: Joint venture with a fintech or start-up with strong credit card product capabilities
Acquire the credit card division of a smaller bank
License or white-label a best-in-class credit card platform

recommendation: Develop a miles loyalty program for PSG's retail credit card customers: award 1 mile per $1 spent, redeemable for domestic and international flights via negotiated airline contracts. This will retain 100% of current credit card customers and stop the ~$500M/year revenue decline in the credit card segment.
Estimated annual program cost is ~$312M/year, well within the $500M/year budget, leaving ~$188M/year for implementation, marketing, and risk mitigation.
Combined with continued organic growth in Commercial and Products and Markets segments, this positions PSG to achieve flat or growing revenues within two years.
risks: Loyalty plan works for competitors but PSG's customers could react differently — uncertain incremental retention effect
Increased demand for flight redemptions could raise negotiated airline costs above estimates, compressing the economics
Additional marketing investment and organizational build-out for the loyalty program could strain execution capacity
next_steps: Run a rapid pilot of the loyalty program across a sample of PSG customer segments to validate retention and redemption assumptions before full rollout
Begin negotiations with major airlines to lock in long-term contract pricing, leveraging PSG's scale (monopsony power)
Assess whether a new internal unit or third-party loyalty platform operator is needed; train marketing leadership on loyalty program best practices
